clue.text: Grace-and-favour water tower offered with ice bath (E&OE) for restoration

annotation.answer: FOR WHAT WE ARE ABOUT TO RECEIVE

indicators.note: a restoration rebuilds something from its parts, so the listed words are rebuilt into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
the letters of the commercial abbreviation 'errors and omissions excepted', without the ampersand

explanation.surface: An estate agent's blurb for a grace-and-favour water tower needing restoration, complete with ice bath and the usual small print.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated 'Grace-and-favour' hides the split: Grace is the definition and favour joins the fodder. E&OE is the disclaimer printed on invoices and sales particulars.
explanation.definitionFit: The words open the traditional Anglican prayer of thanks said before a meal, the standard example of saying grace.

clue.text: Did she grow to support the Young Pretender?

definitions.text: Did she grow to support the Young Pretender?

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who raised plants, the plant life of a region being its growth
setter's reading: the Jacobite heroine MacDonald who helped Bonnie Prince Charlie escape after Culloden

explanation.surface: A question whether some woman's gardening helped the cause of Charles Edward Stuart.
explanation.walkthrough: Flora MacDonald smuggled the Young Pretender, Bonnie Prince Charlie, to Skye in 1746; the word also names the plants that grow in a place.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the Jacobite heroine doubles as the collective term for vegetation growing in a region.

clue.text: A la what, Marcel? Bit over the top, isn't it?

definitions.text: Bit over the top, isn't it?

blocks.note: first meaning: the missing word in Proust's title 'A la ... du temps perdu'

blocks.clueFragment: Bit over the top, isn't it?
blocks.note: second meaning: overly refined, far-fetched or precious

explanation.surface: Someone asks Marcel Proust about his title and complains his style is a touch excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: Marcel Proust's novel is 'A la recherche du temps perdu'; the same French word is used in English for something affectedly refined.
explanation.definitionFit: Recherché fills the gap in the novel's title and in English describes something studied, exotic or excessively elaborate.

clue.text: Add herb oil, mixed and seasoned

indicators.note: things mixed are stirred together, so the given letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction: pour in herb oil, stir and season the dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seasoned' looks like more cookery, but it means experienced and tough.
explanation.definitionFit: A hard-boiled person is tough and cynical through long experience, as a seasoned veteran is.

clue.text: Distress you, brother? Bit over the top, isn't it?

definitions.text: Distress you, brother? Bit over the top, isn't it?

blocks.note: surface reading: asking a monk whether something upsets him; setter's reading: dis-tress, removing a monk's hair

blocks.clueFragment: Bit over the top, isn't it?
blocks.note: setter's reading: the shaven patch is a bit on the top of the head

explanation.surface: Someone asks a friar whether it upsets him and suggests it was all rather excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Distress' as dis-tress, taking the tresses away: a monk's crown is shaved as a sign of his order.
explanation.definitionFit: The shaven crown of a monk's head is exactly a bald bit on the top that has lost its tresses.

clue.text: Otorhinolaryngologists here let one out on licence

definitions.note: loose: entitle means give a licence or right to

indicators.note: out suggests something put out of place, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat specialism
Roman numeral one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hospital department where ear, nose and throat doctors release a patient on parole.
explanation.walkthrough: The long medical word is the setter's joke: it simply means ENT doctors.
explanation.definitionFit: To entitle someone is to grant them a right or permission, as a licence does; the definition is loose.

clue.text: One propelling through the prison system?

definitions.text: One propelling through the prison system?

blocks.note: first reading: a ship's propeller, which drives a vessel through water
second reading: a prison warder, who moves inmates through the system

explanation.surface: Someone who pushes offenders through the prison system.
explanation.walkthrough: Screw is British slang for a prison officer, and also the name for a ship's propeller.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's propeller is called a screw, and in British prison slang a warder is a screw.

clue.text: Slant society put on the royal bloomers

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for society
Kew Gardens in London is the Royal Botanic Gardens, home of countless flowering plants

explanation.surface: High society puts on the queen's underwear at a slant.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomers are flowers here, not knickers; Kew is the royal botanic garden in west London.
explanation.definitionFit: A skew is a slant or oblique angle, and to skew something is to slant it.

clue.text: Take top off evergreen with hammer

indicators.note: removing the top of a down entry means dropping its first letter

blocks.note: privet is an evergreen hedging shrub

explanation.surface: A gardener lops the top off an evergreen hedge with a hammer.
explanation.definitionFit: To rivet is to hammer out the end of a metal pin so it fastens plates together.

clue.text: Something of the 1 down's rave-up, say?

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the phrase and write down a different spelling of the same sound

blocks.note: a rave-up is a wild party, a wild time

explanation.surface: A question about part of Flora's riotous party.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 down is FLORA, the plants of a region; this herb is one of them, and also blows on Oberon's bank in 22.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild thyme is a creeping herb of British heaths, one member of the native plant life.

clue.text: Old Bill, the past and former king

blocks.note: once means at some time in the past
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: The police, their history and a deposed monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Bill is British slang for the police, but here it means a banknote no longer issued.
explanation.definitionFit: A oncer was slang for the one-pound note, a bill of currency withdrawn in Britain in 1988.

clue.text: Hazel's assailant, a madman we find despicable

blocks.note: a nut is a crazy person
taken as written
evil means wicked and despicable

explanation.surface: Hazel's attacker is a lunatic everyone finds contemptible.
explanation.walkthrough: Hazel looks like a woman's name, but it is the hazelnut tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The nut weevil is a beetle whose larvae bore into and eat hazelnuts, so it attacks the hazel tree.

clue.text: See 1
Neat how it adds up

indicators.note: up turns the preceding word over, so it is read from its last letter to its first

blocks.note: to tot is to add up a column of figures

explanation.surface: A tidy explanation of how a sum is reached.
explanation.walkthrough: Neat is not tidy but an old word for cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: A stot is a young bullock or steer, and neat is the archaic collective word for oxen and cattle.

clue.text: The fruit of smelted copper slag

indicators.note: smelting melts ore down and recasts it, so the letters are melted and reformed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The product of melting down copper waste.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrog is a dialect word for a stunted bush, and its apple is the small sour wild crab apple, a fruit.

clue.text: See 1
It goads horses to take up slower jumping!

indicators.note: jumping letters leap out of their places and land in a new order

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for recipe, Latin for take
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rider's spur makes horses that are slow over the fences pick up the pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumping' sounds like show-jumping in this horsey scene, but it stirs the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A rowel spur has a small spiked wheel at the heel that a rider presses into a horse's flank to urge it on.

clue.text: Palindromist's punt?

blocks.note: setter's reading: a palindrome reads the same in both directions
surface reading: a bet, here one placed to win or finish in the places

explanation.walkthrough: Punt here is a bet, not a boat; this kind of bet covers both a win and a place, as a palindrome works in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: An each-way bet backs a horse both to win and to be placed, and suits someone who writes words reading both directions.

clue.text: How do you fancy women? That could be tabu, love! Put a lid on it!

indicators.note: could be offers another possible form of the words, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for women
lid is slang for a hat
taken as written
love is zero in tennis scoring, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Someone propositions a woman, is told that sort of thing is taboo, and is told to shut up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put a lid on it' sounds like 'be quiet'; the lid is a hat, placed on what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are ways of suggesting something to someone: 'what about a drink?' means 'how do you fancy a drink?'.

clue.text: At which point, wife confronts her age

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
taken as written
an eon is an age, a vast stretch of time

explanation.surface: The moment a wife faces up to how old she is getting.
explanation.definitionFit: Whereon is a formal relative adverb meaning upon which, used of the place or moment something happens.

clue.text: Refusnik's Nietzschean input means nothing at all in Natal

indicators.note: an input is something put inside, so the letters sit within the words around it

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A Soviet dissident borrows Nietzsche's nihilism: nothing at all matters.
explanation.walkthrough: Natal is a South African province, and the answer is South African slang from Afrikaans.
explanation.definitionFit: In South African English, from Afrikaans, niks-nie means absolutely nothing, nothing whatsoever.

clue.text: No amateur supporter, 'e would find it insulting

blocks.note: someone who is not an amateur is a professional
a fan supports a team
the dropped-aitch pronoun loses its H, leaving the letter alone

explanation.surface: A professional football follower would find some remark offensive.
explanation.definitionFit: Profane language is irreverent and blasphemous, which insults what others hold sacred.

clue.text: Saw something of Solomon

blocks.note: first meaning: a saw is an old saying or maxim
second meaning: one of the sayings collected in the biblical book traditionally attributed to King Solomon

explanation.surface: King Solomon offered to cut a baby in half; this seems to recall the blade he would have used.
explanation.definitionFit: A pithy wise saying is a saw, and the Book of Proverbs is ascribed to King Solomon.

clue.text: This depends on the listener

blocks.note: surface reading: whatever it is relies on the person hearing; setter's reading: it hangs down
setter's reading: the listener is the ear itself, from which the fleshy part hangs

explanation.walkthrough: Depends is used in its old literal sense of hangs down, and the listener is the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The soft fleshy lower part of the outer ear hangs from it, so it literally depends from the organ of hearing.

clue.text: Forces out air disasters

blocks.note: first meaning: puffs, exhales hard through the lips
second meaning: setbacks, heavy shocks or misfortunes

explanation.surface: An account of plane crashes involving the armed forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forces' and 'air' suggest the RAF and air crashes, but it is a verb phrase for puffing.
explanation.definitionFit: One blows when expelling breath, and blows are sudden calamities or setbacks.

clue.text: "____, 17 the 8 21" (Oberon's reassurance for no-account dreamers?)

blocks.note: fill-in: Oberon's line in A Midsummer Night's Dream, completed with the answers to 17, 8 and 21
setter's reading: comfort for people with no bank account, offered in a play about dreams

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is 'I know a bank where the wild thyme blows'; the bank is a grassy slope, but the clue reads it as a bank for the account-less.
explanation.definitionFit: Oberon speaks the line in A Midsummer Night's Dream, and taken literally it promises a lender to the unbanked.

clue.text: Minogue's missile one found in a Scottish strait

indicators.note: found in places one item inside the other

blocks.note: a kyle is a narrow sound or strait in Scotland
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: The pop star's projectile is discovered in a channel off Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Kylie Minogue supplies the name; the word is also an Australian Aboriginal term for a boomerang.
explanation.definitionFit: In Western Australia a kylie is a boomerang, a thrown weapon, and it is also the singer's first name.

clue.text: Mrs Copperfield's war-time confinement measure

blocks.note: first meaning: the first name of Spenlow, David Copperfield's first wife in Dickens
second meaning: the Defence of the Realm Act, the 1914 law that restricted civilian life

explanation.surface: A wartime restriction once imposed on David Copperfield's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Confinement looks like childbirth for Mrs Copperfield, but it is the restrictions of the 1914 Act.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Dora Spenlow becomes David's wife, and DORA is the acronym of the Defence of the Realm Act.

clue.text: Ordain him, for example, at church

blocks.note: him is an example of a pronoun
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A bishop consecrates a priest during a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: Ordain looks like making someone a priest, but it means decree.
explanation.definitionFit: To pronounce is to declare or decree formally, as a judge pronounces sentence, and to ordain is to order officially.

clue.text: Stalk the prince and the baker's daughter

blocks.note: PR is an abbreviation for prince
Ophelia in Hamlet says 'They say the owl was a baker's daughter', from a folk tale

explanation.surface: A prince pursues the baker's girl, like a fairytale.
explanation.walkthrough: In the folk tale a baker's daughter was turned into an owl for meanness to Christ, which Ophelia recalls in Hamlet.
explanation.definitionFit: To prowl is to move stealthily in search of prey, much as one stalks it.

clue.text: Cultist seeking return of an emperor

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the words that follow are read backwards

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article, a
a tsar was the emperor of Russia

explanation.surface: A member of a sect hopes their emperor will come back.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitting, since Rastafarians revere the Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie.
explanation.definitionFit: A Rasta is a follower of Rastafarianism, a religious movement whose members venerate Haile Selassie.

clue.text: Inspire once to have me bear the disruption

indicators.note: a disruption throws things into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone once inspired another to put up with the upheaval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks the answer as an archaic word.
explanation.definitionFit: To embreathe was an old verb meaning to breathe into, the literal sense of inspire.
